name: Street Custom 'Last Word' Ring Gun
description:
A single-shot firearm built into an oversized ring worn on the index or middle finger, firing a .22 short round from a barrel concealed within the ring's decorative setting. The weapon is activated by pressing the palm-side trigger plate with the thumb while the hand is clenched into a fist. The round fires forward from the ring face, roughly aligned with a pointing gesture. Accuracy is nonexistent beyond 2 meters, but at contact range — pressed against a target's body during a handshake, an embrace, or a struggle — the weapon is lethal.

Last Word rings are handmade in the Shelf by jeweler-gunsmiths who have combined their crafts into a single, desperate art form. Each ring is unique, built around whatever firing mechanism and barrel stock the maker can acquire. The external appearance ranges from crude metal bands to surprisingly sophisticated designs that mimic legitimate jewelry. The best makers produce rings that pass casual inspection, with firing mechanisms hidden behind gemstone settings that swivel aside to reveal the barrel.

The weapon has a grim reputation because of the circumstances of its use. Nobody carries a ring gun as a primary weapon. It is the weapon you carry when you expect to be searched, expect to be held at gunpoint, and expect that the only chance you'll get is when someone comes close enough to touch. It is named the Last Word because it is intended to be used when every other option has been exhausted.
specifications:
caliber: .22 Short
capacity: 1 round
effective range: Contact to 2 meters
weight: 30-60g depending on construction
form factor: Oversized ring, worn on index or middle finger
tactical_use: Absolute last-resort weapon for contact-range use when all other options have failed. The Last Word is carried as insurance against scenarios where the user will be disarmed, restrained, or cornered. Its single round must count.
cultural_context: The Last Word ring is a Shelf institution. Owning one means you live in a world where you might need to kill someone with your hands. The rings are sometimes given as gifts between people who work dangerous jobs — runners, couriers, debt collectors — as a gesture that says 'I want you to come home.' The craftsmanship of the ring reflects the maker's regard for the wearer.
known_users: Anyone who expects to be searched
story_hooks: A corporate security executive was killed by a .22 Short round fired at contact range during what appeared to be a handshake. The shooter was a Shelf resident who had been brought in for 'questioning.' Nobody checked the rings.

A master ring-maker in the Shelf has started producing Last Words with a twist — the ring contains a microphone and transmitter that activates when the firing mechanism is charged, broadcasting a final recording to a preset recipient. People are using them to send messages from beyond the grave.

physical_description.visual_profile: An oversized signet or statement ring that could plausibly pass as avant-garde jewelry at casual glance. The form factor is deliberately deceptive — it reads as an expensive accessory rather than a weapon, with the barrel concealed behind a swiveling gemstone setting or ornamental face. The ring sits heavy on the finger, slightly unbalanced toward the palm side.
physical_description.dimensions: Ring band width: 12-18mm, setting diameter: 20-28mm, barrel depth: 8-12mm. Worn on index or middle finger, extending 15-22mm above the knuckle when clenched.
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and substantial despite small size — 30-60g creates noticeable presence on a single digit. The weight distribution is intentionally forward-heavy, pushing toward the setting where the barrel sits. In a closed fist, it creates an asymmetrical feel that takes practice to conceal naturally.
physical_description.primary_material: Mixed metals — base band is typically surgical steel, titanium, or black-market exotic alloys. Barrel stock salvaged from disassembled firearms (often irregular sourcing). Gemstone or ornamental face is faux or low-grade real stone, functioning as both camouflage and mechanism housing.
physical_description.finish: Highly variable by maker. High-end examples feature polished steel with brushed accents, mimicking legitimate jewelry. Mid-tier rings show signs of hand-fabrication with file marks visible under close inspection. Budget versions appear crude and rough, with visible welding seams and uneven metal work. All examples show wear quickly — micro-scratches accumulate on the setting from repeated palm-side manipulation.
physical_description.color_scheme: Predominantly gunmetal gray, matte black, or brushed steel. Accent colors include gold or copper plating on band edges (for higher-end examples), or dull silver where multiple metals are joined. Gemstone faces range from clear/white (diamond simulant) to deep red (synthetic ruby) or black (onyx), depending on maker aesthetic and available materials.
physical_description.grip_texture: The band itself is smooth metal, slightly cold to the touch. The setting swivel mechanism is deliberately designed for thumb access — textured just enough to prevent slipping during the firing motion, but subtle enough to read as normal jewelry wear. Some makers add microscopic ridging or light etching. The interior band (palm-side) may be slightly rougher or padded with thin synthetic material to reduce slipping.
distinctive_features: Swiveling gemstone or decorative face that rotates 90-180 degrees to expose barrel
Hidden palm-side trigger plate — subtle depression or raised bump that thumb activates
Asymmetrical weight distribution creating distinctive feel when worn
Fine capillary scratches around setting from repeated access and handling
Possible maker's mark stamped inside band — initials, symbol, or serial number visible only when removed
Firing pin mechanism partially visible inside setting if closely inspected
Varying quality of metal joins and welding — higher-end rings show seamless work, street versions show obvious seams
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Street Custom rings rarely bear maker identification externally — this is intentional for plausible deniability. Makers often stamp a personal symbol or initials inside the band, invisible unless ring is removed. Some high-end jeweler-gunsmiths carve microscopic initials near the setting hinge. Black-market rings may bear nothing, or cryptic maker's marks that function as authentication tokens in the Shelf underworld.
physical_description.condition_typical: Even new examples show hand-fabrication marks under magnification. Field-worn rings develop distinctive micro-damage patterns: light scratches on the setting from repeated swivel access, discoloration around the trigger plate from sweat and oils, faint impression marks on the band where the ring was gripped during practice firing. Well-maintained examples show protective patina, while neglected ones develop corrosion at metal joins. The setting mechanism becomes slightly loose with use, developing a faint click if swiveled with pressure.
